quote: If man were never to fade away like the dews of Adashino, never to vanish like the smoke over Toribeyama, but lingered on forever in the world, how things would lose their power to move us!
source: Yoshida Kenkō, Essays in Idleness, section 7 (trans. Donald Keene, 1967)
note: Corrected the wording: Keene writes lingered on forever in the world, not in this world. The citation to section 7 of Keene's 1967 translation is otherwise right.

evidence.where: a transcription of Keene's selections headed Essays in Idleness, The Tsurezuregusa of Kenko, section 7 read in full, checked against Wikiquote citing Keene 1967 section 7; the Columbia volume itself was not opened
evidence.edition: Essays in Idleness: The Tsurezuregusa of Kenkō, trans. Donald Keene, Columbia University Press, 1967

reason: The sentence is the famous opening of section 7, but two independent witnesses of Keene's text read in the world where the proposal has in this world, so the wording is corrected to Keene's. The section's later sentences turn bleak about old age; the opening sentence stands alone. Kenkō is at 2 of 3 and is also proposed in the fiction-essay lane, so only one can land.
